In the UK and its colonies (including Australia and Canada), it's known as Armstice or Remembrance day. A very popular thing for people to do is to wear a plastic poppy, in reference to a famous poem about soldiers dying upon Flanders field. The date itself references the signing of the treaty of Versaille ending WW1. This recent Canadian commercial is a nice homage to it: Poppy

It's not generally a national holiday, but schools generally hold a brief assembly regarding it. Note that the UK and colonies don't really have an equivalent to memorial day, but this is their day to mourn those lost in the two World Wars and the conflicts after in general. Otherwise there's memorial services, but to my knowledge it isn't a full holiday. Here is video from the service from last year

I've always been fascinated by this, long studying books on the subject even though I was so ill through much of my childhood that I seriously doubted I would live to see the turn of the century. While I realized that the more fanciful impressions of the future in the media were unlikely, I was often frustrated by the potential so casually thrown away by politicians, corporations, and our own primitive obsessions. I hoped to one day work in space or live in a 'town' like Disney World's Contemporary Hotel. (you can't get much cooler than door-to-door monorail service) Being pretty science and tech savvy, there were few surprises. The persistence of the idea of the telephone, as opposed to voice communication as a computer application, was unexpected. The smartphone seems anachronistic as I foresaw the mobile phone evolving into something simpler and more elegant while that form-factor would be assumed by mobile computers. It doesn't make sense to me that people are still putting touch screens up against their face and that we're still talking about phone companies. I expected the advent of Ubiquitous Computing would see the much sooner obsolescence of the conventional desktop computer and feel the hegemonies of the anachronistic phone companies is largely responsible for that. The persistence of the conventional Operating System is similarly puzzling as we were commonly talking about much simpler architectures and very different user interface metaphors in the past. Document-oriented computing was long considered the near-future. I also expected Personal Rapid Transit technology to be implemented before the advent of self-driving automobiles. That seemed rather ridiculously overcomplicated and costly given the much simpler solutions that had been well demonstrated even in the 1970s. But the conservative war on public transportation and renewable energy has compelled that more overcomplicated solution.

It was that charming but shifty rogue King Alexander I of Macedon (known, with ironic ambiguity, as 'the Philhellene') who finally made up the Greeks' minds for them. The message he sent them was brief and to the point. Their present position was untenable. They would be cut off and massacred by Xerxes' vastly superior forces. His philhellenism was given a somewhat dubious flavour by the fact that his brother-in-law happened to be a Persian general, a connection he was at some pains to explain away; but his main concern had little to do with nationalism or ideologies. What really bothered Alexander was the prospect of Xerxes' army being held up indefinitely in Macedonia, a plague of human locusts stripping the granaries bare, decimating herds and flocks. The sooner they were on their way the better; and that meant ensuring that they found no entrenched opposition awaiting them at Tempe.

You will always have half of your genetic material from your mother, half from your father, but due to crossing over, each sperm or egg has a different half each time. Your siblings, therefore, could be as much as 100% equal to you (identical twins, or impossible luck), or 0% equal to you (also impossible luck).

tl;dr Parents and kids are always share 50% of each other's DNA, siblings share 0-100% (but likely closer to 50%).

yes, in theory, its possible for sibling to have 100% or 0%, but that would be very very rare just because the number of random recombinations that occur. because so many genes cross over between paired chromosomes, it actually comes very close to 50% since random error decreases due to increased size. its like if you toss a coin thousands of times, it is most likely going to be around 500 heads and 500 tails.. it would be very rare to have 0 heads and 1000 tails..
